The source places CAN below WAN in scale.
The source presents these as alternative terms rather than distinct technologies.

value.misconception: CAN is just a larger single LAN.
value.correction: The source defines CAN as an interconnection of LANs, so its defining structure is aggregation/interconnection of local networks.

value.misconception: CAN is larger than a MAN.
value.correction: The source explicitly states CAN is smaller than MAN.

value.misconception: CAN always means wireless networking.
value.correction: The source emphasizes switches, routers, optical fiber, copper plant, and Cat5 cabling; wireless is not required by this definition.

value.misconception: CAN equipment must be externally owned.
value.correction: The source says equipment and transmission media are almost entirely owned by the campus tenant/owner.

value.misconception: Only universities use CANs.
value.correction: The source explicitly includes enterprise, university, and government ownership/use contexts and discusses corporate campuses.

value.misconception: A CAN has to use fiber.
value.correction: Fiber is one named medium; copper plant and Cat5 are also explicitly named.

value.misconception: Every campus CAN must use 10 Gigabit Ethernet.
value.correction: 10 Gigabit Ethernet is one example of high-speed Ethernet, alongside Gigabit Ethernet.

value.misconception: The 1–5 km figure is an absolute universal standard.
value.correction: The source states this range but marks the associated statement with a citation-needed note; it should be treated as source-provided rather than a universal engineering rule.

value.misconception: Campus network and corporate area network are completely different technologies.
value.correction: The source presents campus network and corporate area network as alternative terminology for CAN.

value.misconception: A CAN is the same thing as the Internet.
value.correction: CAN is a limited-area network interconnecting LANs; the Internet is separately listed as a much broader network category.

value.summary: A machine-readable knowledge graph covering clearnet terminology, its relationship to the Internet and World Wide Web, surface/deep/dark web distinctions, search indexing, IP-address exposure, anonymity networks, privacy considerations, technical context, and source provenance.

value.primary_input: User-supplied text of Wikipedia article Clearnet (networking)
value.method: Core claims are attributed to the supplied article; additional networking and privacy explanations are labeled background or external_reference.
limitations: The supplied Wikipedia page is marked as a stub and provides limited technical detail.
The three references in the supplied article are historical, so they should not be treated as current operational-security guidance.
An IP address does not by itself prove the identity of a natural person.
Clearnet is used inconsistently: broad usage refers to the public Internet, while narrow usage refers to the indexed surface web.

dimensions.name: accessibility
dimensions.description: Whether a resource can be reached without credentials or specialized network software.

dimensions.name: indexability
dimensions.description: Whether conventional search engines can discover and retrieve a resource.

dimensions.name: network_path
dimensions.description: The route used to reach a destination.

dimensions.name: privacy_linkability
dimensions.description: How readily activity can be linked to a user; depends on multiple signals and the threat model.

ordinary_clearnet_request_flow.action: The user initiates a request to a public website.
Packets are forwarded toward the destination; network operators may observe some connection metadata.
A hostname may be resolved to an IP address; resolver visibility depends on resolver and transport configuration.
Traffic reaches hosting, CDN, reverse-proxy, or origin infrastructure.
TLS protects application traffic in transit between TLS endpoints, but does not conceal all metadata from every observer.
The service processes the request and may receive source address, cookies, account state, and request data.
Operators may log or correlate requests subject to configuration, policy, and law.

anonymity_network_flow.action: The client connects using anonymity-network software.
The entry relay sees the client connection but ordinarily does not know the final destination when Tor is correctly used.
Traffic is forwarded through the circuit.
Public Internet traffic may leave through an exit relay; onion services use Tor's onion-service mechanisms rather than a conventional public-Internet exit.
The destination generally sees the exit address for public-web traffic or the Tor-mediated connection for an onion service, not the client's ordinary public IP.

caveats: These are conceptual flows, not packet-level protocol specifications.
Exact routing depends on the network, protocol, DNS setup, browser, and destination type.
Anonymity networks do not guarantee immunity from endpoint compromise, account-based identification, user disclosure, configuration mistakes, or traffic correlation.

similarities: Often used interchangeably in casual terminology.
differences: Clearnet may mean the public Internet broadly; surface web more specifically means indexed web content.

similarities: Both may be absent from ordinary search-engine results.
differences: Deep web is defined mainly by non-indexing and can include ordinary database portals; dark web usually refers to services hosted on anonymity-oriented networks.

similarities: Both can improve aspects of security or privacy.
differences: HTTPS protects traffic content between endpoints; an anonymity network changes routing and may reduce destination visibility of a client's network address. Neither alone guarantees anonymity.

similarities: Both can affect what address a destination sees.
differences: A VPN generally routes traffic through one provider's egress infrastructure; Tor uses a multi-relay anonymity network. Their trust models and protections differ.

potentially_observable_data: source IP address as seen by a destination or intermediary
request metadata available at relevant endpoints
browser/device characteristics that contribute to fingerprinting
DNS or connection metadata visible to relevant network operators
caveats: Not every website collects or retains every listed data type.
An observed IP address may belong to a shared gateway, VPN, proxy, mobile carrier NAT, or other intermediary.
HTTPS reduces exposure of application content to passive network observers but does not prevent the destination from seeing the request.
Privacy depends on observer position, endpoint security, configuration, provider practices, and legal environment.
threat_model_questions: Which party is the user trying to hide information from: destination website, ISP, local Wi-Fi operator, advertiser, employer, or state-level observer?
Is the goal to hide content, IP address, identity, location, or browsing relationships?
Is the user logged into an identifying account?
Can the endpoint and browser be trusted?
What metadata remains visible at each network hop?

value.title: Cloud Computing — Full Relationship-Rich Semantic Knowledge Graph
value.purpose: A detailed graph of cloud-computing concepts, service models, architecture, dependencies, providers, economics, operations, security, privacy, standards, history, and legal context.
value.source_policy: The supplied Simple English Wikipedia extract is authoritative for source-derived claims. Modern provider and architecture concepts are marked as synthesis. No external web research was performed.
value.temporal_caveat: Provider/product examples in the article are historical. They are preserved as source-era examples, not as a current market ranking.
value.provenance_policy: Line numbers refer to the extracted source lines. Empty line lists identify concepts added as explanatory synthesis.

value.graph_design: Directed typed relationships express mechanisms, dependencies, roles, constraints, examples, and distinctions rather than generic related_to links.

value.name: Cloud service abstraction
value.description: Provider-operated infrastructure is abstracted through virtualization and service interfaces so consumers can use capabilities without managing every physical detail.

value.name: Service-model stack
value.description: IaaS exposes infrastructure; PaaS exposes a platform; SaaS exposes an application. Provider responsibility generally increases at higher abstraction levels.

value.name: Typical cloud application dependency graph
value.description: Illustrative modern dependency chain; not every component is explicitly discussed in the source.

value.name: Usage and cost
value.description: Measured consumption supports usage billing and cost visibility; total cost still depends on usage and pricing.

value.name: Reliability and recovery
value.description: Redundancy, replication, backups, failover, and tested recovery can reduce failure impact but do not guarantee zero downtime or data loss.

value.name: Cloud security responsibility
value.description: Provider and consumer responsibilities vary by service model; identity, access, encryption, and compliance remain key concerns.

value.name: Architecture and interoperability
value.description: Cloud components communicate through APIs and web services; compatible interfaces can improve interoperability.

value.name: Provider lock-in and portability
value.description: Managed services reduce operational burden but may create provider-specific dependencies that increase migration effort.

value.name: Data jurisdiction
value.description: Global cloud deployments cross legal borders; region, data handling, contracts, and applicable law influence compliance.

value.name: History described by the source
value.description: The article traces utility-computing ideas to 1960, cloud terminology to the early 1990s, AWS access in 2002, and wider research/mainstream attention in 2007–2008.

value.difference: Service delivery versus distributed computation across loosely coupled machines.
value.why_it_matters: A cloud may use grid techniques, but the terms are not synonyms.

value.difference: Service abstraction versus measured consumption and billing.
value.why_it_matters: Usage billing alone does not define cloud computing.

value.difference: Service delivery versus systems capable of self-management.
value.why_it_matters: Automation can be a characteristic but is not the entire cloud model.

value.difference: Operating cloud systems versus selling enabling products or services.
value.why_it_matters: An organization can play both roles, but responsibilities differ.
The model changes which layers the consumer operates.

value.difference: Application deployment platform versus hosted application.
value.why_it_matters: Building on a platform differs from consuming finished software.

value.difference: Changing capacity versus consistent operation and failure handling.
value.why_it_matters: A scalable system can still experience outages.

value.difference: Historical examples versus a current market comparison.
value.why_it_matters: The source does not establish present-day market share or provider quality.

value.difference: Operational abstraction versus coupling to provider-specific APIs and behavior.
value.why_it_matters: Managed services trade operational work against migration flexibility.

value.misconception: Cloud computing is just another name for the Internet.

value.misconception: Cloud computing and grid computing mean the same thing.

value.misconception: Every cloud service is billed only by usage.

value.misconception: Cloud computing eliminates all infrastructure costs and operations work.

value.misconception: Cloud scalability means outages cannot happen.

value.misconception: Centralizing data always improves security.

value.misconception: Cloud deployment guarantees compliance everywhere.

value.misconception: Multi-cloud automatically reduces cost and complexity.

value.question: Define cloud computing.
value.answer: A model where storage, processing, platforms, or applications are delivered by an external or managed provider and accessed over a network.

value.question: What does the electricity analogy explain?
value.answer: Consumers use a utility without managing how it is produced and delivered.

value.question: How does grid computing differ?
value.answer: Grid computing distributes tasks across loosely coupled computers; cloud computing is a service-delivery model.

value.question: What is utility computing?
value.answer: Measured compute or storage resources billed according to use.

value.question: What is autonomic computing?
value.answer: Systems designed to manage themselves to some degree.

value.question: What is multitenancy?
value.answer: Multiple consumers share underlying resources while being logically separated.

value.question: How can multitenancy improve utilization?
value.answer: Shared resources can serve workloads that would otherwise leave capacity idle.

value.question: Why can cloud reduce peak-load overprovisioning?
value.answer: Consumers can obtain extra capacity from a provider rather than own capacity for every peak.

value.question: What is the difference between IaaS and PaaS?
value.answer: IaaS delivers infrastructure; PaaS delivers a platform/solution stack for deploying applications.

value.question: What does SaaS deliver?
value.answer: A hosted software application.

value.question: What role does virtualization play?
value.answer: It abstracts physical resources into logical environments that can be allocated as services.

value.question: What is an SLA?
value.answer: A service-level agreement specifying service-quality expectations or commitments.

value.question: Does an SLA mean perfect availability?
value.answer: No. Outages can still occur; an SLA defines commitments or remedies.

value.question: Name cloud storage categories from the source.
value.answer: Database-like services, NAS, synchronization, and web/object storage.

value.question: What does the source say about storage metadata?
value.answer: Metadata operations may be centralized while data nodes scale independently.

value.question: Why can bandwidth affect cloud performance?
value.answer: Cloud clients depend on network connectivity; insufficient bandwidth or high network load can degrade response.

value.question: What can redundant sites support?
value.answer: Reliability, business continuity, and disaster recovery.

value.question: What is one limit of redundancy?
value.answer: It does not guarantee uninterrupted service, and customers may have limited control during provider outages.

value.question: Why does cloud raise privacy concerns?
value.answer: Providers may access, alter, delete, or disclose hosted data under policies or legal processes.

value.question: What is data residency?
value.answer: The location where data is stored or processed.

value.question: What is data sovereignty?
value.answer: Legal authority and jurisdiction that apply to data and systems.

value.question: How does a provider differ from a vendor?
value.answer: A provider operates cloud systems; a vendor sells products or services enabling cloud delivery.

value.question: Which providers does the source name?
value.answer: Google, Amazon/AWS, Yahoo!, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, HP, and SAP, among others.

value.question: What does the article associate with AWS in 2002?
value.answer: Amazon opened access to its systems through AWS on a utility-computing basis after data-center modernization.

value.question: What idea does the source attribute to John McCarthy in 1960?
value.answer: That computation might someday be organized as a public utility.

value.question: Name some standards listed by the source.
value.answer: HTTP, XMPP, OAuth, OpenID, SSL/TLS, Atom, AJAX, HTML5 offline, OVF, LAMP, XML, JSON, and REST.

value.question: What was AGPL intended to address according to the source?
value.answer: A perceived loophole involving modified free software run over a network.

value.question: Why can managed services increase lock-in?
value.answer: Applications may depend on provider-specific APIs, data models, identity systems, or operational behavior.

value.answer: How an application depends on compute, networks, storage, identity, databases, queues, and observability.

formal_models.name: Cloud service abstraction
formal_models.description: Provider-operated infrastructure is abstracted through virtualization and service interfaces so consumers can use capabilities without managing every physical detail.

formal_models.name: Service-model stack
formal_models.description: IaaS exposes infrastructure; PaaS exposes a platform; SaaS exposes an application. Provider responsibility generally increases at higher abstraction levels.

formal_models.name: Usage and cost
formal_models.description: Measured consumption supports usage billing and cost visibility; total cost still depends on usage and pricing.

formal_models.name: Reliability and recovery
formal_models.description: Redundancy, replication, backups, failover, and tested recovery can reduce failure impact but do not guarantee zero downtime or data loss.

formal_models.name: Cloud security responsibility
formal_models.description: Provider and consumer responsibilities vary by service model; identity, access, encryption, and compliance remain key concerns.

formal_models.name: Architecture and interoperability
formal_models.description: Cloud components communicate through APIs and web services; compatible interfaces can improve interoperability.

formal_models.name: Provider lock-in and portability
formal_models.description: Managed services reduce operational burden but may create provider-specific dependencies that increase migration effort.

formal_models.name: Data jurisdiction
formal_models.description: Global cloud deployments cross legal borders; region, data handling, contracts, and applicable law influence compliance.

formal_models.name: History described by the source
formal_models.description: The article traces utility-computing ideas to 1960, cloud terminology to the early 1990s, AWS access in 2002, and wider research/mainstream attention in 2007–2008.
